---
title: "SQL in Positron"
description: "Write and run SQL in Positron. Link each .sql file to a data connection for table and column completions and warnings for unknown names, and run statements in a ggsql console."
---

SQL support in Positron builds on [Data Connections](data-connections.qmd). When you link a `.sql` file to one of your data connections, the file gets table and column completions from that database, hover information, warnings for names the database does not have, and links to the **Data Connections** view.

You can also run the statement under the cursor with {{< kbd mac=Command-Enter win=Ctrl-Enter linux=Ctrl-Enter >}}, as you do in [Python](guide-python.qmd) and [R](guide-r.qmd). Statements run in a [ggsql](https://ggsql.org) console connected to the same database.

::: {.callout-important}
SQL support is an experimental feature, and you must turn it on. Enable the [`sql.enabled`](positron://settings/sql.enabled) setting. The change takes effect without a reload.
:::

## Choose a connection for a file

Positron links each `.sql` file to one data connection. The connection determines which tables and columns Positron offers and the SQL dialect it uses to parse the file.

The status bar shows the connection for the active `.sql` file. Click it, or run _SQL: Select Data Connection_ from the Command Palette, to choose a different one. The list includes your saved connections, plus an **Automatic** option.

With **Automatic**, the default, a file uses the only open data connection. If more than one connection is open, or none are, choose one for the file. Until a file has a connection, Positron completes SQL keywords only and does not warn about unknown names.

Positron remembers the connection for each file, including after you rename it or save it under a new name. When you open a file that you linked to a connection, Positron opens that connection for you. To connect by hand instead, for example when a connection asks for credentials or starts a billed warehouse, disable [`sql.connectOnOpen`](positron://settings/sql.connectOnOpen).

## Write SQL

Once a file has a connection, Positron reads the connection's schema and uses it as you type:

- **Completions**: Positron offers the names that fit where the cursor is. It offers tables after `FROM` and `JOIN`, and columns from the tables the statement reads, including columns from a common table expression (CTE) defined with `WITH`. After a qualifier such as `orders.` or an alias, it offers only that table's columns.
- **Warnings**: Positron flags table and column names that are not in the connection's schema, along with syntax errors. Positron does not flag aliases or CTE names that the statement defines.
- **Hover**: Hold the pointer over a table to see its columns, or over a column to see its type.
- **Links**: {{< kbd mac=Command win=Ctrl linux=Ctrl >}}-click a table or column name to reveal it in the **Data Connections** view.

If you create or change tables after Positron reads the schema, run _SQL: Refresh Database Schema_ from the Command Palette to read it again.

::: {.callout-note}
For very large databases, Positron reads only part of the schema. In that case, completions can be missing some tables, and Positron does not warn about unknown table names for that connection.
:::

### SQL dialect

Positron parses each file in the dialect of its connection's driver, so quoting, string escapes, and comments follow the rules of that database. A file without a connection uses a generic dialect that accepts most SQL. To use the same dialect for every `.sql` file, set [`sql.dialect`](positron://settings/sql.dialect).

The Positron SQL parser does not cover the full grammar of every database, so some valid SQL can show a syntax warning. For example, the DuckDB `ASOF JOIN` and `USING SAMPLE` clauses produce a warning even though they run.

## Run SQL

To run SQL, place the cursor in a statement and press {{< kbd mac=Command-Enter win=Ctrl-Enter linux=Ctrl-Enter >}}. Positron runs that statement only, even if it spans several lines, and then moves the cursor to the next statement. To run part of a statement, or several statements at once, select the text first. You can also run _SQL: Run SQL Statement_ from the Command Palette.

Statements run in a ggsql console connected to the file's database:

- If a ggsql console is already connected to that database, the statement runs there.
- Otherwise, Positron starts a new ggsql console, connects it to the database, and then runs the statement.

Positron never reconnects a ggsql console to a different database, because reconnecting discards any in-memory data in that console. Files linked to different databases each get their own console.

A statement can include a ggsql visualization after its query, for example, `SELECT ... VISUALISE x, y DRAW line`. {{< kbd mac=Command-Enter win=Ctrl-Enter linux=Ctrl-Enter >}} runs the query and the visualization together, and the plot appears in the [Plots pane](plots-pane.qmd). See the [ggsql documentation](https://ggsql.org) to learn the syntax.

::: {.callout-important}
Positron does not bundle ggsql. To run SQL, [install the ggsql extension](https://ggsql.org/get_started/installation.html). If it is not installed, Positron shows a notification that offers **Install ggsql**.
:::

### Supported databases

You can run SQL against DuckDB, SQLite, MotherDuck, PostgreSQL, Redshift, and ODBC connections. ggsql reaches PostgreSQL and Redshift through ODBC, so you also need the ODBC driver for that database installed.

You cannot run SQL against Snowflake or Databricks connections, or against MotherDuck on Windows. Completions, warnings, and hover still work for these connections.

If a statement does not run, Positron shows a notification with the reason, for example, when the file has no connection or ggsql cannot connect to the database. When ggsql reports a connection error, the details appear in the **Console**.

::: {.callout-note}
DuckDB allows only one process to open a database file for writing. If the same DuckDB file is open in the **Data Connections** view, running SQL against it fails with a lock error. Collapse the connection in the **Data Connections** view to disconnect it, and then run the statement again.
:::

## SQL in Quarto documents

In a [Quarto](quarto.qmd) document, `{sql}` code cells get the same completions, warnings, and hover as `.sql` files. A Quarto document is not linked to a data connection, so SQL cells use the only open data connection. If more than one connection is open, or none are, SQL cells get keyword completions only.

{{< kbd mac=Command-Enter win=Ctrl-Enter linux=Ctrl-Enter >}} does not run SQL cells in a ggsql console. Running statements in ggsql works in `.sql` files only.

## Settings

- [`sql.enabled`](positron://settings/sql.enabled): Turn on SQL support for `.sql` files. Disabled by default.
- [`sql.dialect`](positron://settings/sql.dialect): The SQL dialect used to parse `.sql` files. **Automatic** (the default) follows each file's data connection. Choose a dialect to use it for every file.
- [`sql.diagnostics.enabled`](positron://settings/sql.diagnostics.enabled): Show syntax errors and unknown names in SQL files. Enabled by default.
- [`sql.diagnostics.unknownNames`](positron://settings/sql.diagnostics.unknownNames): Show a warning for table and column names that are not in the file's data connection. Enabled by default.
- [`sql.connectOnOpen`](positron://settings/sql.connectOnOpen): Open a file's data connection when you open the file. Applies only to files you linked to a connection. Enabled by default.
